CO2016A-GE-41.exp: Reading the underlined word as 'on', it is a preposition linking 'effect' to 'one's health'. Confidence is low because the underlining was lost in extraction; note that across questions 39-44 each item's answer is a different part of speech, and 'Preposition' appears here but not in Q42's options, which points to 'on'.

CO2016A-GE-42.exp: Reading the underlined word as 'supported', it is the main verb of the sentence (present perfect 'have supported'). The underlining was lost in extraction, so this rests partly on the run 39-44 testing one distinct part of speech each, with Verb the category left for this item.

CO2016A-GE-43.exp: 'Yesterday' here modifies the verb 'came', telling when the action happened, so it is an adverb of time. The classic trap is calling it a noun - it can be one ('yesterday was hot'), but not in this position. The underlining was lost in extraction.

CO2016A-GE-44.exp: 'Green' is an adjective used as an objective complement, describing the resulting state of 'her hair'. The trap is 'Adverb', since a word following a verb is often adverbial - but here it describes the object, not the action. The underlining was lost in extraction.

CO2016A-GE-45.exp: 'Since last week' marks an action that started in the past and is still going on, which calls for the present perfect continuous: have been missing. Plain present perfect 'have missed' is defensible for a set of completed instances, so the item is not watertight.

CO2016A-GE-46.exp: 'By the time' + present tense sets a future deadline, and the action is completed before that point, so the future perfect 'will have arrived' is required. 'Had arrived' wrongly puts a future event in the past perfect.

CO2016A-GE-47.exp: 'Since graduating' fixes a starting point in the past running up to now, which demands the present perfect: has had. The past perfect 'had had' would need a second, later past reference point, which the sentence does not supply.

CO2016A-GE-48.exp: The question mark requires inverted interrogative order, which rules out 'You will take', and future perfect makes no sense here; 'Will you take' is the standard simple-future question and request form. 'Will you be taking' is grammatically possible, which keeps this from being a clear-cut item.

CO2016A-GE-49.exp: The sentence has just one finite verb, 'came', with the rest being phrases ('to me', 'with his starving family'), so it is a simple sentence containing a single clause. No conjunction or subordinate clause is present.

CO2016A-GE-50.exp: Two independent clauses - 'I could not come' and 'I was down with fever' - are joined by 'for', which traditional grammar classes as a coordinating conjunction giving a reason. Two coordinate main clauses make the sentence compound.

CO2016A-GE-51.exp: 'Finishing my book' is a participial phrase, not a clause, since it has no finite verb; the sentence's only finite verb is 'placed'. One finite clause means a simple sentence.

CO2016A-GE-52.exp: At the top level two independent clauses are coordinated by 'but', which makes the sentence compound; the relative clause 'who demanded more' is merely embedded in the second of them. Strictly this is a compound-complex sentence, and since that label is not offered, 'compound' is the closest available answer.

CO2016A-GE-53.exp: 'Which was red in colour' is a subordinate relative clause depending on the main clause 'I have sold my car'. One main clause plus a subordinate clause makes the sentence complex.

CO2016A-GE-54.exp: 'That I gave you yesterday' is a relative clause qualifying the noun 'money', and a clause that does an adjective's work of describing a noun is an adjective clause. It is not a noun clause because it does not itself function as subject or object.

CO2016A-GE-55.exp: 'Which was stolen' qualifies the noun 'book', doing the work of an adjective, so it is an adjective (relative) clause. The main clause is 'The book ... was mine'.

CO2016A-GE-56.exp: 'Since I came here three days ago' modifies the verb by telling when the illness began, so it is an adverb clause of time. 'Since' is here a subordinating conjunction of time, not a coordinator.

CO2016A-GE-57.exp: 'That you have succeeded' is the object of the verb 'to know', and a clause filling a noun's slot is a noun clause. Substituting 'it' ('I am happy to know it') confirms the clause is doing a noun's work.

CO2016A-GE-58.exp: 'Wherever he went' modifies the verb 'carried' by stating place, making it an adverb clause of place. 'Wherever' is a subordinating conjunction of place.

CO2016A-GE-59.exp: 'Did not fail to turn up' is a double negative, so the sentence in fact asserts that he did turn up - the notion is affirmative and the sentence is assertive (declarative). 'Negative' is the trap, describing only the surface form 'did not', not the meaning conveyed.

CO2016A-GE-60.exp: The 'That ... should ...!' pattern with a final exclamation mark expresses strong feeling, here indignation, making it an exclamatory sentence. It states no fact and issues no command, so it is neither assertive nor imperative.
